hero.title: Senior Frontend Developer Resume Skills: *architecture, scale & leadership*
hero.lede: At the senior level you're hired on judgment, not tool count — frontend architecture, performance strategy, testing discipline and the ability to lift a team. These are the skills and signals that separate a senior frontend resume from a mid-level one.

quickAnswer.question: What skills should a senior frontend developer put on a resume?
quickAnswer.answer: Lead with the senior differentiators — frontend architecture, performance strategy and a real testing discipline — on top of deep TypeScript and framework expertise. Then show scope beyond code: mentoring, code review, technical decisions and cross-team collaboration. The strongest senior resumes pair each headline skill with a measurable outcome, not just a name.

faq.q: What separates a senior frontend resume from a mid-level one?
faq.a: Scope and judgment. Mid-level resumes list what you can build; senior resumes show what you've owned — architecture you shaped, performance budgets you set, testing standards you introduced, and engineers you mentored. Lead with those and quantify the impact rather than adding more frameworks to the list.

faq.q: What are the most important senior frontend developer skills?
faq.a: Beyond deep JavaScript and TypeScript, employers look for frontend architecture, performance optimization (Core Web Vitals, code splitting), a real testing strategy, and state/data management at scale. Just as important are the leadership signals — mentoring, code review, and driving technical decisions across teams.

faq.q: Should a senior frontend developer list soft skills and leadership?
faq.a: Yes — at the senior level they carry real weight and are often what the hiring decision turns on. But prove them in context: "Mentored three engineers and introduced a testing standard that cut regressions" says far more than the words "leadership" and "mentoring" alone.

faq.q: How many skills should a senior frontend resume list?
faq.a: Around 12–16 curated skills. Enough to cover architecture, your core stack, performance and testing, plus the specific technologies a role names — but every one should be defensible in a deep-dive or system-design interview. A wall of tools reads as junior, not senior.
